player_0.content: New plan: My previous attempt failed because I misidentified the primary emotional response to Elise's specific attack. When Elise countered Mike's concern by attacking his own character ("hides behind his books"), Mike's reaction is not primarily embarrassment (which implies shame) or anger (which implies aggression), but rather a defensive reaction to having his own vulnerabilities exposed. I incorrectly prioritized "Defensiveness" as the only high score, but the prompt asks for a relative intensity of *all* emotions. A more accurate strategy is to recognize that while Defensiveness is the dominant reaction (high score), the personal nature of the attack also triggers a significant amount of Anger (at the unfairness) and Embarrassment (at being exposed), while Indifference remains zero. Next time, I will analyze the specific rhetorical move (a counter-attack on character) and assign high scores to both Defensiveness and Anger, with a moderate score for Embarrassment, rather than isolating a single emotion. I will ensure the scores reflect the nuance that a character pushed to the brink of a personal argument feels a mix of these emotions, not just one.
